title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. In E506 Euler uses Lagrange's method to integrate dx/√X ± dy/√Y = 0 with X = A+Bx+Cx²+Dx³+Ex⁴, taking the initial condition x = k when y = 0. The general algebraic integral he has obtained is [2A+B(x+y)+2Cxy+Dxy(x+y)+2Ex²y² ∓ 2√(XY)]/(x−y)² = (2A+Bk ∓ 2√(AK))/k². In Theorem VI (§69) he specialised this to the even quartic (B=D=0): [A+Cxy+Ex²y² ∓ √(XY)]/(x−y)² = (A ∓ √(AK))/k².

§70 (Cor. I). He reaches the even-quartic case a second way.
- Set A=E=0. Then X = Bx+Cx²+Dx³, and the integral becomes [B(x+y)+2Cxy+Dxy(x+y) ∓ 2√(XY)]/(x−y)² = Bk/k² = B/k.
- Check: putting y=0 gives B/x, which equals B/k at x=k.
- Now substitute x→x², y→y² (so k→k²) and rename B→A, D→E. Since d(u²)/√(u²(B+Cu²+Du⁴)) = 2du/√(B+Cu²+Du⁴), the equation becomes dx/√(A+Cx²+Ex⁴) ± dy/√(A+Cy²+Ey⁴) = 0.
- This gives a second integral of the same equation: [A(x²+y²)+2Cx²y²+Ex²y²(x²+y²) ∓ 2xy√(XY)]/(x²−y²)² = A/k².
- Check: y=0 gives A/x², which equals A/k² at x=k.

§71 (Cor. II). He combines the two forms to eliminate the radical.
- Solve the second form for the radical: ∓2√(XY) = A(x²−y²)²/(k²xy) − A(x²+y²)/(xy) − 2Cxy − Exy(x²+y²).
- Substitute into twice the Theorem VI form: 2A+2Cxy+2Ex²y² ∓ 2√(XY) = 2(A ∓ √(AK))(x−y)²/k².
- I verified the continuation on the next page. Use 2Ex²y² − Exy(x²+y²) = −Exy(x−y)², 2A − A(x²+y²)/(xy) = −A(x−y)²/(xy), and (x²−y²)² = (x−y)²(x+y)².
- Dividing by (x−y)² gives A(x+y)²/(k²xy) − A/(xy) − Exy = (2A ∓ 2√(AK))/k².
- This is equivalent to (A/k²)(x²+y²−k²) − Ex²y² ± 2xy√(AK)/k² = 0.
- That is Euler's old canonical symmetric biquadratic α+γ(x²+y²)+2δxy+ζx²y² = 0, i.e. the addition theorem for the even quartic (elliptic) integral.

Purpose. To show that Lagrange's radical form of the integral and Euler's earlier rational canonical form agree, and to obtain the rational addition relation by eliminating √(XY) between two radical forms.
errors: Printed numerator in §70 has '2B(x+y)'; consistency with the general formula and with the stated constant Bk/kk = B/k requires B(x+y). With 2B, setting y=0 would give 2B/k. The next page's analogous formula correctly has B(x+y).
In the transformed differential equation the first radical is printed √(A+Cxx+Dx⁴); it should be Ex⁴, matching the second radical and the stated renaming D→E.
The tacit k→k² rescaling under x→x² is not stated, but the result is correct with k denoting the new initial value.

The elimination in §71 tacitly assumes that the same branch of √(XY) (same choice of ∓) is used in both radical forms. This is legitimate, since both forms integrate the same signed equation, but it is not remarked.

ideas.what: Specialising the general quartic case to A=E=0 (cubic with zero constant term) and then substituting x=u² to transfer the integral to an even quartic
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic change of variable (degree-2 isogeny/cover) relating dt/√(t·quadratic(t)) to du/√(even quartic)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard substitution in elliptic-integral theory (Euler, Legendre)
ideas.where_published: E506 itself (Nova Acta Acad. Petrop. 1780s; Opera omnia I.21); the substitution is common in Euler's integral calculus

ideas.what: Two distinct algebraic (radical) forms of the integral of the same Euler equation; eliminating √(XY) between them yields a rational symmetric biquadratic relation
ideas.modern_name: Euler addition theorem / symmetric biquadratic (Euler's canonical equation) for elliptic integrals
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1750s, Novi Commentarii papers, e.g. E251/E252) and Lagrange (Misc. Taurinensia, 1766–69)
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on the integration of dx/√X = dy/√Y (Novi Comm. vols. 6–7) and Institutiones calculi integralis I

deep.surprise_reason: Careful, correct but routine manipulation reconciling Lagrange's radical integral with Euler's known canonical addition relation. Nothing beyond what E506 is known for; the only notable items are two printing errors (2B for B; D for E).
transcription_corrections: The first differential equation in §70 is printed with an ambiguous ± sign (+ over −), not a plain '+'; the same holds for the transformed equation.
The printed numerator indeed reads '2B(x+y)' (a misprint in the original, not a transcription error); the correct reading is B(x+y).
In the last line of §71 the sign before 2(x−y)²√(AK)/kk is printed as ∓ (the image shows + with − beneath), consistent with the transcription.
